The point is that the utxoset ballooning from 4GB to 12GB has made it no longer feasible to use a RPi 4B as a bitcoin node, whereas before the recent spam attack, it worked just fine.

elements.text:
A snapshot is a flushed copy of the table heads, concurrent with the flush to disk of all table bodies. A snapshot looks exactly like the “head” subdirectory and rotates between a “primary” and “secondary” folder. This ensures that once there is a good snapshot, a failed future snapshot can always revert to the previous good one.

The purpose is to allow the store to revert to the point where the snapshot was taken, in the case of a process fault (uncontrolled termination). I also use it in development to roll the store back to certain points (such as post-sync and pre-validate, by storing a snapshot once synced, though on big machines we sync and validate concurrently).

The node knows for sure when a previous shutdown has not been completed, and when it starts up will automatically recover
from the most recent snapshot

. If there is no snapshot it will currently require a manual restart after clearing the store. This gives us full fault tolerance, which leveldb (and most  general database systems) cannot actually provide. This is pretty extraordinary given that the store is fully write/write and read/write concurrent.

A snapshot of the full store took 68 seconds cold and 37 seconds warm, and full stop took 35 secs. Restore from snapshot took 22 seconds. For those who are new to BN, snapshots can be performed hot (without a stop), and the full store can be hot-backed up to a snapshot point(s).

Yes, we have complete indexes in addition to validation metadata. The two "validated" tables are disposable, and in the case of reorgs would just get generated as necessary. Essentially they are state repositories that assist with concurrency. The "strong" table is not disposable, and only provides the reverse index from (confirmed) tx to its confirming block. This gets overwritten (to negative) in the case of a reorg out of the block.

Navigation is possible from candidate or confirmed height to header, header to parent, header to txs (if block is stored), txs to spends (sequence) and outputs (script/value), spend to input (contains script/witness), input to point (output natural key), output to containing tx, spend to containing tx, tx to confirming header (and position in its block).

This can cause a few seconds of delay in each download “window” as the last work is shuffled around, but a peer cannot delay the sync. The window can also be configured to be the whole chain, but breaking it up is good for preventing validation delay.

elements.text: Query performance is critical, and my tests show that we are orders of magnitude faster than ElectrumX and Fulcrum (and no doubt BC but I haven't tested). Making a node useful means providing features that are always being bolted on to bitcoind. We provide the full chain Electrum address index during sync, for about 30 mins extra presently. That takes ElectrumX and Fulcrum up to a week when operating against a fully-synced and local bitcoind. So where is the performance issue? probably both. The ability to expose the node to high volume query is important, as otherwise yet again it requires full extraction to a capable query server making the node much less usable. We worked through this in BS in versions 1-3 using ZeroMQ and it's mature. Yet another one of Amir's solid design decisions (same with proactor async and mmap hashmap store).

elements.text:
Libbitcoin isn't just a node, it's a developer toolkit. It has significant public API. The code is intended to document itself, including the behavior of Bitcoin over its history. We don't remove old behavior. New forks are additive, so that they can be disabled/enable by the user/developer. This preserves the history and exposes the behavior. These are significant undertakings in addition to just writing a node, server, or client stack.

The script machine is place to learn exactly how Bitcoin works, which few people would ever be able to do using bitcoind, and there are no compromises on performance. In order to get more out of script, we implemented a variant stack, which eliminates state stack type conversions in all standard scripts, and templatized the stack data structure (and compile with both std::vector and std::list), which resolves the quadratic op_roll issue.

To simplify maintenance and centralize optimization of hashing functions, we implemented the entire hashing stack from spec in C++ templates, and benchmarked it against bitcoind optimizations. It tends to outperform as a consequence of improved use of compiler auto-vectorization. There's no longer any C code in the library (though we do embed qrencode, which is C). Dropping in SSE, AVX2, and AVX512 was trivial (I don't believe Core has AVX512 yet), and we'll get SNANI and ARM variants added as well, in the same template.

These are investments that are starting to pay off. The code has been absurdly reliable, which was not the case in the old days. This has made it possible to keep pushing forward without having to look back as we used to have to do a lot. But it took years to get to this point. We still have a way to go, but people are starting to notice. And that's good, because there needs to be some group that speaks for maintaining the decentralized nature of the design even if it isn't quite ready yet. I have spoken up about these types of design issues for years. But it goes nowhere, which I understand. Code talks, and Cypherpunks write code.

This shows a very consistent time difference (lag) between the buffering of each job and the completion of validation of the net block. The buffering progression is initially ordered from 1-850k, but the validator is asynchronous, so completion is out of order within what is buffered.

Initially with very small blocks, the validator is fast enough to preclude any backlog (note that the x axis is not time-based but block height-based, so the first 1/5th of the graph completes in one minute).

The backlog starts accumulating until it hits the arbitrary 1024 * 5000 tx limit (configured). Then it is cycling back to zero delay before reaccumulating a backlog. This is because the validator owns the CPU while it works off all of the jobs, and its completion handlers don't execute until all the backlogged jobs are complete.

This implies some amount of waste as the CPU drops off the peg momentarily in order to get the backlog restarted. However without a limit the backlog would include a job for every block. The tx count that imposes the limit is read directly from the store, not from the deserialized block, since of course the limit is imposed prior to the read/validate job.

The waste can be seen infrequently in the perf monitor as narrow CPU slices that drop off the 100% peg. Ideally we would want to be always buffering jobs while validating, but we need a limit and that's hard to measure if the stranded job completion handler invocation is blocked by the ongoing work.
